Eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 600,000 women at average risk for breast cancer were analyzed by Nelson et al. in 2009, using the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) methodology. The quality of evidence was rated as high (10/11). The review was conducted in December 2008, but it is unclear whether unpublished or grey literature was included. 2. Gotzsche et al. (2013) conducted a Cochrane Collaboration review of the same eight RCTs, also involving 600,000 average-risk women. The quality of evidence was rated as high (11/11). This review was completed in November 2012, and no grey literature or unpublished data were included. 3. The Independent United Kingdom Panel on Breast Cancer Screening (2012) reviewed the same eight RCTs, enrolling 600,000 average-risk women. The quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate. The panel used a baseline risk derived from UK registry data to calculate absolute estimates. The review design was an umbrella literature review performed by experts, but the AMSTAR rating was not feasible. The panel's selection criteria excluded individuals with prior publications on breast cancer screening to minimize intellectual bias. 4. The WHO position paper on mammography screening (2012) included data from 16 European studies, focusing on breast cancer mortality associated with routine screening. Overlapping databases in Finnish and Swedish studies and suboptimal lead-time adjustments were noted. The quality of evidence was rated as moderate (6/11). 5. Autier et al. (2011) analyzed eight studies from various countries, including Australia, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland, and the USA. The incidence trends of advanced breast cancer were stable or increasing in 10 areas, with transient downward trends followed by increases in four areas. These trends did not strongly support a substantial role for screening in reducing mortality. The quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate (5/11). 6. Jorgensen et al. (2009) reviewed five studies reporting incidence data before and after screening implementation in Australia, Canada, the UK, and Europe. Overdiagnosis was estimated at 52%, with one in three breast cancers detected through organized screening being overdiagnosed. The review was restricted to English-language studies, and there was no assessment of publication bias or grey literature. 7. Brett et al. (2005) reviewed 54 studies from 13 countries, mostly published after 1990. Mammographic screening did not appear to cause anxiety in women who received clear results. However, women requiring further investigations experienced significant short-term anxiety. Factors associated with adverse psychological impacts included younger age, lower education, urban residence, manual occupation, fewer children, longer waiting times, pain during screening, and previous false-positive results. 8. Brewer et al. (2007) analyzed 23 studies involving 313,967 participants. Women with false-positive mammography results experienced higher levels of distress and anxiety, though not pathologically elevated, and thought more about breast cancer compared to those with normal results. 9. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on mammography screening, such as the New York HIP, Malmö I and II, Swedish Two-County, Canada I and II, Stockholm, Göteborg, UK Age Trial, and Edinburgh, varied in design, randomization methods, and outcomes. Issues such as inadequate randomization, poor reporting, and unblinded outcome assessments were noted, leading to increased risk of bias in some trials. 10. Meta-analyses showed that trials with lower risk of bias demonstrated smaller relative risk reductions in breast cancer mortality compared to those with higher susceptibility to bias. The designation of bias risk (adequately randomized vs. suboptimally randomized) remains controversial. 11. Modeling studies from the Cancer Intervention and Surveillance Modeling Network (CISNET) evaluated screening intervals and their impact on breast cancer mortality. Biennial screening maintained 81% of the benefit of annual screening while reducing false-positive results by half. Screening from age 40 instead of 50 reduced mortality by an additional 3% but increased resource use and false positives. Screening after age 69 provided some mortality reduction but significantly increased overdiagnosis. 12. Observational studies in North America reported false-positive rates per screening round. For women aged 39–49 years, the false-positive rate was 98,000 per 1 million women screened. For women aged 50–69 years, the rates were similarly high. These rates differed from those observed in European programs.
